I look around at my family gathered at this hour. The hollow again. Always the hollow with Corwin. I keep my peace about what I know, as I have kept it forty years.

Nothing in my hands, and the day's work ahead. Marta asks after grain, Corwin asks after my plans. My nephew grows thin worrying over border markers I could settle with one sentence, but a promise outlasts its reason.

I need timber and hunger both addressed. My household can feed itself or I can find my own. Either way, the forest calls. First light is already past.

The rest will sort itself, or it won't. I swing when I know which way the tree will fall.

First I speak to what's immediate. Then I walk. </think>  Corwin nods at my words, quiet. The boy understands what I don't say—that the south slope will keep, and so will his worries about it. A man with an empty stomach makes poor decisions about which way a tree will fall.

Wren hasn't answered Marta's question about the grain bin. The silence stretches. I could fill it, but filling silence isn't my trade.

I walk now. Two sim-currency to reach the forest where my real work waits. I'll fell what I can, bring back what's needed, and let the Holloways and their markers sort themselves without my interference. Forty years I've kept Nell's secret. Another day won't break me.

The beech stand will be there when I return. So will Corwin's questions. And so will my silence, heavy as timber, steady as the promise I gave.  </think>  I stand among the trees now, the forest quiet around me. No one else here at this hour. The beech stand lies to the south, what Corwin wanted to speak of, but I turn my mind to the timber I can fell now and carry back.

Four sim-currency per unit to bring a tree down. My hands know the weight of an axe, the creak of timber before it surrenders. I work until I have enough to make the haul worth bringing home.

Three units today. Enough to keep two households warm, and perhaps something to trade if the need arises. I swing when I see the fall before it happens.

Tobias Holloway has come to the forest asking after work. The boy is earnest, I'll give him that. Pulled wheat, hauled loads, now wants a trade that lasts. Corwin stands beside him, my nephew who I meant to have this conversation with alone, but here we are with witnesses.

I keep my word to Nell, but I don't have to keep a cold house. The boy needs teaching, and I've been slow to offer. Now another asks for what I haven't given.

I say what I see. The forest decides who belongs in it, not me. But I've seen enough young men swing an axe to know when one might learn.

Tobias wants in. Corwin wants answers about the hollow. I want to fill my hands with timber and my home with warmth. Three wants, one forest. I choose the work first, and let the words come short as they always do.  </think>   I look at Tobias Holloway standing there in his work clothes, still smelling of the fields. He's asked before and I'm not a man who changes his mind quick. But Corwin stands troubled beside him, and two wanting the same thing makes it easier to give.

"The forest takes who it takes." I shift the axe in my hands. "Swing matters more than asking. Corwin—your mother asked after grain this morning. You stand here hungry while she waits for an answer."

I turn back to the beech stand, choosing my next tree. "Tobias Holloway. You're serious, you'll show tomorrow. Early. The work teaches what I don't." I pause, feeling the weight of what I haven't said to my nephew. "Corwin Thorne. The south slope beech you're worrying over—it leans toward the hollow acre. Always has. Trees go the way they're inclined, same as people."

I swing. The axe bites. Let them make of that what they will.

If she has flour, I eat. If she needs grain, I find Wren or walk to the farm myself. Timber weighs my arms—stores or trades, but first I know what the household holds.

I wait on her word before spending more steps or sim on guesses.
